news.title: From the front row to the hot seat — what the midterms mean for Big Tech
news.text:
Right before the midterm elections, OpenAI hired Jessica Schumer, daughter of Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer. The company also said it would start calling its data centers “compute campuses.”

For the past two years, many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names have built closer ties with President Donald Trump and his administration. Several attended White House events, some companies scaled back diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and some executives donated millions to super PACs supporting his campaign and allied candidates. Administration policies also benefited the industry, including tax breaks, the pausing of some federal investigations, and looser AI regulation. Meanwhile, Meta faced lawsuits and billion-dollar fines, and OpenAI faced suits alleging its technology harmed users.

Now, with the midterms shifting the balance of power in Washington, those same companies are working to rebuild ties with Democrats, who have pledged to tighten oversight of AI. How far that gets them may depend less on image-polishing than on where the real fights are happening: in state capitols, in communities deciding whether to host data centers, and, as we’ve seen this past week, in the markets watching the AI boom.

J.B. Branch, director of federal AI governance and technology policy at Public Citizen, a nonprofit advocacy group that describes itself as nonpartisan, told me that the tech industry “realizes they have an optics problem.” He characterized moves like the Schumer hire and the rebranding as “PR washing.” He expects more of it, too, pointing to OpenAI’s partnership with the American Federation of Teachers, announced last year, as well as Anthropic’s newly launched Claude Corps and Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. “I would imagine more of that sort of investment in these corporate, private-public partnerships,” he said.

These initiatives didn’t spring up overnight. Meta and other tech companies reportedly began looking for ways to strengthen their ties to Democrats as Democratic gains in the midterms looked more likely. Reached for comment about the midterm elections’ impact on Meta, a company spokesperson pointed TechCrunch to remarks that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick made this week at WSJ Tech. “You have to work with the government that the American people elect,” McCormick had said. “I have seen it across the board that you have to be bipartisan, and you want to be, because you want buy-in on the things that you’re trying to do.”

Not everyone expects them to work. Alice Marwick, director of research at the tech policy nonprofit Data & Society, told me she expects Big Tech to try to pivot back toward the middle, “if not the left. But it’s a little too late,” she said. “Tech companies should be asking themselves how their products can make people’s lives better, because right now, it doesn’t seem like they are.”

If Democrats follow through on pledges to tighten oversight of AI and Big Tech, the industry could face a tougher environment. Data center moratoriums are gaining traction, and a wave of AI regulation bills awaits drafting. At the same event, Powell McCormick said Meta wants to show that communities welcoming its investments will see “an enormous amount of benefit,” while those that don’t want them “will of course have the right to stop them.”

Still, the next two years could bring political gridlock in Washington. Aryan Ranjan, founder of Baraza, a political campaign management software company, told me most action will likely happen at the state level, since states have already sued tech companies and passed regulations. “A coalition built on newer, working-class voters is likely to push Democrats to frame AI around electricity bills, data-center siting and jobs rather than abstract AI safety,” he said of what to expect at the federal level.

Last December, the Trump administration signed an executive order creating the AI Litigation Task Force, a federal group meant to challenge state AI laws. The administration has argued that U.S. AI companies “must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulations.” Many states have nonetheless passed their own laws, including measures on chatbots and deepfakes.

It also remains to be seen how President Trump will respond, including whether he’ll sign more AI executive orders or veto bills that could be seen as anti-AI. Clearly, voters want stronger guardrails around the technology.

In a statement to TechCrunch, a White House official said: “American leadership in super intelligence is essential for our national security, economic prosperity, and the quality of life of the American people. President Trump is committed to ensuring America continues to lead the world in super intelligence while protecting American consumers. As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.” 

Branch argued that Trump’s political fortunes are now tied to the AI industry. On Wednesday, the day after the midterms, a trillion-dollar market sell-off spooked investors, some are whom are reportedly now reconsidering Anthropic’s reported trillion-dollar IPO. “There’s a very strong likelihood that there will be an AI bubble pop, and it’ll happen on Trump’s hands,” Branch said, predicting a possible market collapse. “Does he want to sink or swim along with the AI industry?”

For now, the rules companies face may vary by location. “For the next two years, a company’s AI rules may depend more on where it operates rather than on anything Washington passes,” Ranjan said.
news.summary: After spending two years getting cozy with the White House, Big Tech is suddenly trying to make friends with Democrats, and the open question is whether that image makeover can hold up against what states, local communities, and the markets are about to do.
news.author: Dominic-Madori Davis

news.title: Venezuelan national arrested near White House with three firearms; says voices told him 'to kill Trump'
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 7 (IANS) A 30-year-old Venezuelan national was arrested near the White House after US Secret Service agents discovered three firearms and ammunition inside a stolen vehicle, with the suspect allegedly telling authorities that voices in his head had instructed him to kill President Donald Trump. The arrest took place shortly before midnight on Thursday when a US Secret Service officer, conducting a routine patrol near the White House, spotted a suspicious blue Ford F-150 pickup truck parked on Constitution Avenue. According to a criminal complaint filed in the DC Superior Court, the officer approached the vehicle and asked the man inside whether he was safe and whether he was carrying any weapons. The suspect, identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, reportedly nodded in response to the question about weapons and made a finger-gun gesture. He subsequently stepped out of the vehicle and communicated with investigators using Google Translate. During questioning, Guanipa Chrinos reportedly told officers that he had a gun because someone had attempted to kill him with it and that he had taken it away from that person. He also directed investigators towards a brown bag inside the vehicle. A subsequent search of the stolen pickup truck uncovered an AR-15 rifle, two handguns and ammunition. According to DHS, the suspect allegedly told officers that voices had instructed him to kill President Trump. He appeared before the DC Superior Court on Friday and remains in custody without bond, according to online court records. DHS identified Guanipa-Chrinos as an undocumented immigrant from Venezuela who entered the United States through Texas in March 2024. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has also lodged an immigration detainer against him. The incident has once again drawn attention to security concerns surrounding the US President and the White House, which remains under heightened security arrangements. Earlier, in April this year, US authorities charged the suspected gunman in the White House Correspondents’ Dinner shooting with attempting to assassinate President Trump, as officials detailed a fast-moving investigation that they said prevented a “massive attack” from unfolding. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said that “that horrible act was stopped because of the courage and professionalism of law enforcement”, adding that “the President and all the protectees and participants at the dinner were safe”. The suspect, identified in court documents as Cole Tomas Allen, faced three federal counts: attempted assassination of the President, interstate transportation of a firearm to commit a felony, and discharge of a firearm during a crime of violence.

news.title: US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
news.text:
LOS ANGELES: The US Department of Justice on Friday requested to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration statuses could be verified.

The move comes days after Republicans’ significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list of alleged noncitizens. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government’s request.

The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump’s administration’s effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with noncitizen voting without providing evidence. Available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare.

The Justice Department remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what it says are suspected noncitizens. It said in a statement Friday evening that it would continue to prosecute and litigate suspected violations of election law through other legal cases.

The department also filed a motion in support of a separate lawsuit filed in May that alleges that California violates national voting laws by failing to sufficiently remove ineligible voters from its rolls. The intervention is part of a broader effort to continue to “pursue every available civil and criminal remedy to ensure that only eligible American citizens vote in American elections,” top Los Angeles prosecutor Bill Essayli said.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably “commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones.”

“The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said.

The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state’s 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels on Friday doubled down on earlier accusations that “California chose to protect illegal voters and thus refused to cooperate” with the federal request to set aside ballots, and said that “thousands of likely noncitizens remain on California’s voter rolls and voted in the 2026 elections.”

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections.

US District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his order that separating ballots at such a late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.
news.summary: The US Department of Justice has withdrawn its lawsuit against California, which aimed to halt the processing of about 20,000 ballots suspected to be from noncitizens. The decision comes ahead of a scheduled hearing to evaluate the accuracy of the voter list.

news.title: USDA to launch AI tool to check crop production data after errors
news.text: The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts.After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview.The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets."I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday.Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3% in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2% in Kansas.The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it reported inaccurate beef export sales data.The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.Computer file errorLance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said."This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level."The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports."You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic."Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data.Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said."The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa. The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.
news.summary: After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview.

news.title: Trump says US talking to Iran amid sanctions push
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump said that Washington was talking to Iran, as his administration imposed sanctions on eight Canadian businesses accused of helping Tehran move money through cryptocurrency networks.

“We’re talking to Iran. We have been,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House.

The president portrayed the military situation as favourable to the United States and said the Strait of Hormuz was opening.

“We’ve beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran,” he said.

Asked for his message to Iran, Trump combined his claim of military success with an indication that diplomatic contacts were continuing.

His comments came on the same day that the Treasury Department announced sanctions against eight Canada-based money services businesses under Operation Economic Outcat.

Treasury accused the companies of exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets to facilitate international transactions involving Iran. It said many had dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges or addresses associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The action was coordinated with Canada’s financial intelligence unit, FINTRAC, the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and the Drug Enforcement Administration, Treasury said.

The sanctions announcement did not describe the measures as part of a negotiated arrangement or identify any connection between the designations and the contacts Trump discussed.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Washington would continue targeting revenue that it alleged supported Iran’s weapons programmes and regional proxies. He said the action reflected cooperation with Canada to protect the North American financial system.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the department would pursue Iran’s financial channels wherever they operated.

Treasury also alleged that several had handled drug proceeds linked to Canadian former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding. Those allegations were set out in the designation announcement; the official material reviewed did not include responses from the businesses.

The measures block designated entities’ property within US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US persons from dealing with them, unless authorised or exempt. They do not amount to a criminal conviction.

news.title: Trump confirms new US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has confirmed US military strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, claiming that Washington has made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran.

Trump said on Friday that US forces had carried out what he described as minor strikes against Iranian air defence systems.

“We do minor strikes,” Trump told reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida. “They knocked out – they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five.”

Trump spoke shortly after Iranian state media reported two missile strikes in the Suza area of Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for oil shipments.

State broadcaster IRIB also reported an Iranian army statement, saying that the country’s air defence forces intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over Qeshm Island.

In response to reports of explosions heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, said the situation is “relatively calm”.

A CENTCOM official told Al Jazeera that they are aware of the reports, adding they have no further comment.

CENTCOM announced in a post on X late on Friday that the US “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

On Monday, Iranian media reported several explosions on Qeshm Island, as American media outlets reported that the US military carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.

Ongoing talks

Trump told reporters several times on Friday that his administration was talking to representatives from Tehran.

“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” the US president said.

“We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran,” he added, without providing details.

On Saturday, Qatar dismissed reports claiming negotiations between the US and Iran have failed, warning that such claims benefit “only those seeking to prolong the war”.

“Promoting such false claims serves only those seeking to prolong the war and destabilise the region,” said Majed al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a post on X.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican Party was dealt a blow in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US. Trump blamed the election results on the Iran war.

Since Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump has shifted between threatening Iran and suggesting that a resolution to the war is near. On Thursday, Trump said the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Unnamed Pentagon officials and military commanders told The New York Times on Wednesday that thousands of US air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the US are poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on Trump’s orders.

Tehran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions from Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.
news.summary: The US president also claims 'a lot of progress' in Washington's negotiations with Tehran.

news.title: Iranian forces 'stronger' than at beginning of war: army spokesman

news.title: Qatar Says PM’s Remarks on US-Iran Talks Were ‘Distorted’ Online
news.text:
Doha: Qatar said that PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani’s remarks were “distorted” online, as several “fake accounts” claimed that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement.

Qatari International Media Office (IMO) said that the Prime Minister’s remarks were distorted to undermine the diplomatic efforts.

“Reports circulating online claiming that His Excellency the Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs stated that the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement are false and misleading. His Excellency’s remarks have been deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability in our region. Many of these claims are being spread by fake accounts trying to undermine diplomatic efforts and push for further escalation. This is deeply irresponsible. His Excellency stated today that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal,” the Qatari IMO stated.

“Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations,” the statement read.

Meanwhile, United States Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at brokering a new ceasefire and resuming stalled nuclear discussions, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.

Behind closed doors, Vance has maintained daily discussions with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir and other mediators, Axios reported.

news.title: Spy targeting Nvidia CEO was alleged China intelligence service recruit: NYT
news.text: The Chinese businesswoman, with whom Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang had alleged ties, was recruited as a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported, citing a memo circulated among policymakers in the Trump administration.On Friday, three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO to address, behind closed doors, the reported links with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of providing information to Beijing, Axios reported.Nvidia has denied the allegations as "baseless".A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre firm named Megaspeed faced intense scrutiny over potential involvement in diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips towards China, as outlined in a report by The New York Times. US authorities reportedly determined that she operated as a Chinese intelligence asset, transmitting information back to Beijing.According to the report, surveillance of the executive, identified as Chinese national Alice Huang or Huang Le, revealed that she maintained a close association with Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang.US President Donald Trump had expressed uncertainty over his confidence in Jensen Huang as an adviser on US technology policy amid the alleged links with the Chinese businesswoman, as per the Washington Post.Speaking to reporters at his annual Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, Trump said he wanted to continue backing Huang but would wait for further information before concluding."I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary," Trump said when asked whether he still had confidence in Huang as an adviser. "I've always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard. But you know, you're dealing in a very complex issue," he added.Trump said he was unaware of the specific intelligence concerns but expressed hope that Huang would be cleared of any suspicion. "We hope everything's okay with Jensen. We'll check it out. We're going to check it out very closely," he said.Calling Huang a "great" and "brilliant" person, Trump added, "When it comes to chips, there's never been anyone like him." As per the report, the Nvidia chief executive successfully lobbied the administration during Trump's second term to reverse stricter export controls governing the company's chip shipments to China. He also finalised a deal with Trump permitting the US government to secure a 25 per cent stake in specific Nvidia processors authorised for sale to China.As the Trump administration considered a comprehensive ban on Nvidia chip exports to China, Huang and his spouse travelled to Mar-a-Lago to persuade Trump to allow technology firms to continue doing business with Beijing.

news.title: JD Vance leads US backchannel talks with Iran to revive ceasefire and nuclear negotiations
news.text: Washington United States Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at brokering a new ceasefire and resuming stalled nuclear discussions, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter. The US vice president’s direct involvement elevates the indirect track to the administration’s highest echelons, underscoring an initiative by Vance to extricate Washington from a conflict he explicitly blamed for the Republican Party’s crushing electoral defeats this week. Vance steps up diplomatic engagement with Iran According to US officials and regional sources cited by Axios, US President Donald Trump currently remains amenable to letting diplomatic efforts proceed to test whether an agreement can be forged. “We’re talking to them,” Trump told reporters on Friday when asked about his message to Iran. Nonetheless, insiders cautioned that should Trump alter course and mandate renewed military action, US forces stand fully prepared to launch strikes on an expedited schedule. Behind closed doors, Vance has maintained daily discussions with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir and other mediators, Axios reported. White House special envoy Steve Witkoff and presidential adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner are likewise engaged in the diplomatic track. Well-informed sources revealed that Vance, alongside Qatari and Pakistani interlocutors, has evaluated setting up a working-level technical meeting involving American and Iranian delegates soon, though such a meeting has not yet materialised. The office of the US vice president chose not to issue any statements concerning the ongoing talks. Vance’s earlier efforts to secure a diplomatic resolution Vance emerged as the most doubtful voice among Trump’s inner circle before the war’s outbreak in late February, persistently pushing for a diplomatic resolution. He previously headed the US negotiating team during an April summit focused on Iran held in Islamabad and played a central role in securing the bilateral memorandum of understanding last June. Vance later led the American delegation for direct talks hosted in Switzerland, which led Tehran to pledge that UN inspectors would be welcomed back to nuclear facilities. However, the resulting agreement collapsed shortly afterwards when units of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed attacks on commercial shipping. New diplomatic initiative seeks to revive negotiations The current diplomatic momentum began gathering pace a fortnight ago when Vance dispatched a formal letter addressed to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a close confidant of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, proposing the resumption of direct talks. Iranian representatives signalled that Vance’s communication generated favourable momentum towards reviving negotiations. On Wednesday, Vance reasserted that the conflict constituted the primary driver behind voters’ rejection of the GOP. While participants involved in the ongoing mediation characterised headway as being made, they depicted the overall pace as extremely sluggish. Trump discusses diplomatic efforts with Qatar Diplomatic engagement persisted on Friday morning as Trump conferred with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani concerning Doha’s efforts to bridge gaps dividing Washington and Tehran. Via an official release from his secretariat, Sheikh Tamim underscored the imperative to “continue dialogue and pursue diplomatic means to resolve differences, spare the region further escalation, and ensure freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies.”
news.summary: Daily discussions with Qatari and Pakistani mediators have gathered pace, although officials describe progress towards a possible agreement as extremely sluggish

news.title: ‘Ceasefire First’: Poland Warns Against US-Russia Deal on Europe’s Security
news.text:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned Friday, Nov. 6, that Ukraine must not be forced into peace negotiations under Russian bombardment, demanding an immediate ceasefire before any discussions on reshaping Europe’s security architecture.

Speaking in Warsaw after a meeting of the Council of the Baltic Sea States, attended by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Sikorski laid out a strict sequence for ending Russia’s war.

“First, a ceasefire, then negotiations on lasting peace, and only afterward possible discussions on restoring Europe’s security architecture and arms control arrangements,” he said.

“No solution can be imposed on Ukraine without its consent and participation at the table. Likewise, Europe’s security cannot be discussed without our involvement.”

His remarks came as Washington prepares to mediate talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week, with President Donald Trump’s administration proposing a broader European security framework involving Moscow.

As Kyiv Post reported, Kallas and Sybiha have also rejected the prospect of Europe being excluded from negotiations determining its security.

Sikorski stressed that countries on NATO’s eastern flank would be particularly affected by any agreement and must have a voice in shaping it.

“Ukraine should not negotiate its future under the pressure of attacks on civilians,” he said, referring to Russia’s continued war crimes and strikes on Ukrainian cities.

The Polish foreign minister also argued that Kyiv currently holds the advantage on the battlefield, emphasizing that Ukraine should not be pressured into accepting Russian demands.

“Strengthening deterrence capabilities is not intended to escalate tensions,” Sikorski said.

“Russia must understand that its continued aggression will carry increasing costs and consequences.”

Poland demands tougher sanctions and Russian tourist visa ban

Sikorski called for an end to Schengen tourist visas for Russian citizens, questioning why Moscow’s nationals continued enjoying freedom of movement across Europe while Russia wages war against Ukraine.

He said Russian citizens received 623,000 Schengen visas in 2025, with 84% issued for tourism.

By comparison, Poland issued just 100 visas to Russians during the same period, primarily to political dissidents on humanitarian grounds, according to Sikorski.

He urged European governments to stop issuing tourist visas to Russians and impose further restrictions on Kremlin-linked individuals, Russian athletes and veterans who fought against Ukraine.

“Russia, which is trying to destroy the European Union from within, should not enjoy the privileges of free movement across Europe,” he said.

Sikorski also called for tougher sanctions against Russia’s shadow fleet and companies supporting its operations.

He urged technology companies and social media platforms to cooperate more closely in countering Russian cyberattacks and information warfare.

“Russia’s sources of financing its war machine must be further restricted,” he said.

Warsaw also supports continued efforts to use frozen Russian assets to finance Ukraine’s defense and reconstruction.

“The aggressor must bear responsibility for the consequences of the war it unleashed,” Sikorski said.

Poland pledges $2 million for Ukrainian generators, prepares military drills

Sikorski announced an additional 8 million zlotys ($2 million) through the Energy Community to purchase generators for Ukraine ahead of winter.

“Our priority is supporting Ukraine’s preparations for the coming winter and strengthening the resilience of its energy sector,” he said.

The announcement comes as Russia continues striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, threatening electricity and heating supplies during the colder months.

Sikorski also highlighted Poland’s role in the Coalition of the Willing, announcing that nearly 2,000 Polish troops would participate in the multinational KOALICJA 26.2 exercises scheduled for Nov. 9-22.

The drills will involve forces from Poland and 11 other countries, preparing for a possible multinational deployment to support Ukraine following a cessation of hostilities.

Poland will also lead support operations for the multinational force.

Sikorski reaffirmed Warsaw’s commitment to Ukraine and European security, emphasizing that Russia must not be allowed to dictate the continent’s future.

“Together, we defend the security of all Europe,” he concluded.

“Peace, sanctions, solidarity.”
news.summary: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski rejected any security agreement negotiated without Ukraine and Europe, insisting on a ceasefire before talks with Moscow. He also demanded tougher sanctions, restrictions on Russian tourist visas and greater support for Ukraine.

news.title: From mass deportations to White House chief, how Stephen Miller became Trump's key pick
news.text: US President Donald Trump has appointed longtime adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, placing one of the architects of his hardline immigration agenda at the centre of his administration as he prepares for an expected political confrontation with Democrats following the Republican Party's losses in the midterm elections.Trump announced the staffing change on Friday, describing Miller as one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller, 41, will take over the role on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles, who has served as chief of staff throughout Trump's second term.The appointment comes as Democrats prepare to launch sweeping investigations into the administration, including its immigration enforcement policies. With Democrats gaining control of Congress, Miller is expected to play a key role in defending the president's agenda and managing the administration's response to congressional scrutiny.Miller's elevation is also being viewed as a sign that Trump intends to maintain his America First agenda rather than retreat from some of his most controversial policies following the electoral setback."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," Miller said on Friday.Why Trump chose Stephen MillerMiller has been among Trump's closest advisers and has played a central role in shaping immigration policy during both of his administrations. His appointment places an experienced policy strategist and a strong advocate of the president's immigration agenda in a key position as the White House prepares for battles with a Democrat-controlled Congress.During Trump's second term, Miller has held a broad policy portfolio but has remained particularly influential in driving the administration's efforts to accelerate deportations of undocumented immigrants, a central promise of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.He also pushed for an expansion of immigration enforcement, including urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to make at least 3,000 arrests a day. In May 2025, he publicly called for a sharp increase in daily arrests, putting pressure on the agency's leadership and widening enforcement beyond immigrants convicted of serious crimes.Miller also proposed deploying the National Guard to support mass deportations and backed the administration's expansion of third-country deportations, under which immigrants were sent to countries where they had neither citizenship nor family ties, including several African nations.His enforcement agenda was supported by approximately $170 billion allocated by congressional Republicans for immigration enforcement and border security under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025.Miller's role in Trump's controversial immigration policiesMiller's influence on Trump's immigration agenda dates back to the president's first term. He helped develop and publicly defend the executive order restricting entry into the United States by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban triggered protests and legal challenges, with its third iteration upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.He was also a leading advocate of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance policy for illegal border crossings, which resulted in thousands of children being separated from their families. Trump eventually backed away from the policy.Miller also pushed for reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual ceiling, setting it at 15,000 for the 2021 fiscal year, then a record low.His policy priorities extended to legal immigration as well. Miller advocated penalising legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it more difficult for them to obtain US citizenship.During Trump's second term, he supported the use of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to expedite the deportation of alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held at the CECOT maximum-security prison. The move triggered a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the administration from immediately deporting Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal.In May 2025, Miller also said the administration was considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court.At a conference in Miami in March 2026, he argued that military force, rather than conventional criminal law enforcement alone, was necessary to defeat drug cartels.He also appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office this summer when the president signed executive orders seeking to deny citizenship to certain children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down an earlier order seeking to end birthright citizenship.Political challenges behind the appointmentMiller's appointment comes at a time when Trump's immigration agenda is facing growing political scrutiny. Although polls in 2024 showed that most Hispanic voters supported mass deportations in principle and backed Trump in large numbers, reports of individual cases of immigration enforcement prompted a backlash within the community.Republicans lost Hispanic support in the midterm elections, undermining expectations of a lasting political realignment in the party's favour. news.title: US offers $29m reward for details on Iran's nuclear program
news.text:
The United States is offering a $US20 million ($29 million) reward "and possible relocation" for information about Iran's nuclear program, the US military says, despite President Donald Trump's repeated claims that it has been obliterated.

A State Department program, Rewards for Justice, "is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran's nuclear program", US Central Command said in a statement on X.

This includes "its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community," it added in the post that appeared on the social media platform on Friday evening, local time.

The program was established in 1984 under the State Department's national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests.

In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations" has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components such as centrifuges.

It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield the reward.

Mr Trump has repeatedly said US forces had effectively obliterated Iran's nuclear program.

"If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East."

But the president also said Iran — which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war — was eager to end the conflict.

"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.

It was the 38th time Mr Trump has insisted that Iran wanted to resolve matters since the conflict began on February 28.

Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting.

And on Tuesday, Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.

Earlier this week, Mr Trump said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site, which Tehran denies is such a facility.

The news came after Iran's air defence force intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over Qeshm Island in the early hours of Saturday morning, according to an army statement reported by state broadcaster IRIB.

The announcement followed reports from Iranian local media that two missiles had struck the island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, conservative Iranian politician Ebrahim Azizi, head of the nation's parliamentary National Security Committee, took to X to warn that the US and Israel would "pay a price" for the ongoing conflict.

"We won't let Trump walk away from the region without paying a price and reparations," Mr Azizi wrote in a post on X.

"Every mistake will be met with a decisive response until we liberate America's largest military base, the Zionist regime, once and for all."

Mr Azizi made the remarks as Iran's supreme leader has ordered the military to update its target bank and respond to any new attack "without geographical limitations".

Iran is reportedly reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the US about Tehran's nuclear program.

The development is raising hopes that the two sides could be inching towards indirect talks on one of the thorniest issues. Mr Trump says this nuclear program issue must be resolved as part of any deal to end the more than eight-month-old war.

Mr Trump on Friday discussed efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East in a telephone call with Qatar's emir, Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani, the Gulf state leader's office said on Friday.

The region remained on edge over the possibility of renewed US military action against Iran in the wake of the Republican Party's drubbing in Tuesday's midterm elections as Mr Trump looked to reassert his authority.

Qatar says the US and Iran should not wait for a "perfect moment" to reach a deal to end the war.
news.summary: A US State Department program, Rewards for Justice, "is offering a $US20 million reward — and possible relocation — for information on Iran's nuclear program".

news.title: US military carries out new targeted strikes on Iran as Tehran's leaders weigh mediator's proposals
news.text: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said the U.S. military on Friday carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system.Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the crucial waterway for oil shipments.Trump in an exchange with reporters described the military action as “minor."“They knocked out -- they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Trump told reporters shortly after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Friday evening.Trump did not offer further details about the target. But U.S. officials have reported that most of Iran’s air defense systems were destroyed or severely degraded during a June 2025 bombardment by Israel and in the early stages of the current conflict. U.S. officials have assessed that Iran would try to rebuild them and other military infrastructure over time.The U.S. military also reported carrying out what it described as defensive strikes on Monday. Explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.Friday's strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican Party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the U.S.The electoral setback — Republicans lost both chambers of Congress — was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the conflict and elevated fuel prices, a byproduct of the war that’s affected nearly every sector of the global economy.In the days since Republicans' shellacking at the polls, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near..Qatar presents new proposals to Iranian officialsEarlier Friday, two Middle East government officials said Iran was reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the United States about Tehran’s nuclear program.But one of the officials stressed that the Iranians, at least at the moment, remain unwilling to engage in negotiations with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.Differences with Iran over its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than 8-month-old war.Both officials were not authorized to comment publicly on the delicate negotiations and spoke on the condition of anonymity.Meanwhile, U.S. Central Command, which oversees U.S. military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the United States was offering “a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above.”The post included a link to the State Department’s Rewards for Justice program.Iran insists on several concessions before nuclear talksThe White House declined to comment about the Qatari-presented proposals on Iran's nuclear program, but Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators' discussions with Iran continue.“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump, who insists the U.S. military remains in control of the conflict with a battered Iran.Yet, Tehran insists on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon..Qataris and Iranians discuss a bridge deal to get to nuclear talksMediators and Iran have discussed a potential bridge deal aimed at helping pave the way for further talks on Tehran’s nuclear program, according to regional officials.They said the proposal, which was recently presented to the two sides by Qatari mediators, called for implementing trust-building measures over the course of two days.These measures include lifting the U.S. blockade and releasing some of the billions of dollars in Iranian frozen funds seized over the years as part of a U.S. campaign to isolate Iran over its nuclear program. In return, Tehran would allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors at its sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel, the officials said.On the second day, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in line with a modified agreement that Iran and Oman have reached on the waterway but has not been approved by the United States, the officials said. That mechanism would be temporary until a permanent deal is reached on the strait in cooperation with other Gulf countries, they said.Following the implementation of the measures, the U.S. and Iran would embark on extensive talks addressing Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium as well as other aspects of its program, the officials said.Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%..Diplomatic efforts pick up following US electionA flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Persian Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the U.S. military to carry out new strikes against Iran.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government.The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defense officials after confirming earlier Friday that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to deescalate tensions.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also held phone calls with his Iraqi and Tunisian counterparts on Friday to discuss tensions in the region. Araghchi and Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein discussed Tehran’s vision for resuming negotiations with the U.S., according to Iraq’s News Agency.Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, who held two calls with Araghchi this week, said Friday in a post on X that it was critical that both sides demonstrate “flexibility” to achieve the “compromise solutions” necessary to prevent the region from sliding into a new wave of escalation.Egypt’s top diplomat also held a phone call with his Emirati counterpart, Abdullah Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to emphasize the importance of political negotiations to prevent another military confrontation that could fuel violence and destruction, according to a statement by Egypt’s Foreign Ministry..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Melania Trump sparks massive security operation ahead of $5M trip to huge Alabama-LSU college football game without the President by her side
news.text:
Melania Trump is set to attend LSU's huge SEC game against Alabama this weekend without her husband, President Donald Trump.

The First Lady is scheduled to attend the game in Baton Rouge, Louisiana and announce a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor, establishing a Fostering the Future endowed scholarship.

And while the President won't be by her side, Melania's presence has sparked a huge security operation with Secret Service at the game and fans warned to expect delays.

President Trump was due to attend the Alabama home game against Georgia last month, only to cancel the trip due to Hurricane Isaias. Earlier this season, he got a roaring reception in Knoxville as he watched Tennessee take on Texas with his wife not making the trip. 

First Lady Melania will now get her own taste of college football without him in one of the biggest games of the week. The couple attended the College Football Playoff National Championship game together in January. 

An announcement from the White House earlier this week said: 'First Lady Melania Trump will travel to Baton Rouge, Louisiana to advance her Fostering the Future initiative with a special announcement at Louisiana State University.

'During her visit, Mrs. Trump will attend the highly anticipated LSU Tigers versus Alabama Crimson Tide football game at Tiger Stadium, where a groundbreaking Fostering the Future campaign will activate across the campus and on the field.'

LSU Athletics sent an email to ticket holders ahead of her appearance, with increased security and campus closures the university warned could change throughout the day at the discretion of the Secret Service.

LSU Athletics said: 'Due to high-profile guests and on-site operations with the U.S. Secret Service, there are security and navigation updates for Saturday's game. Please allow extra time for parking, campus navigation, and reaching your seat.'

LSU junior Wynter Allen is set to receive a $10,000 scholarship funded by Melania's program and be recognized alongside the First Lady at Tiger Stadium.

He told WAFB9: 'I mean, it's exciting, it's nice to be able to meet the person who's changed my life and hopefully continues to. Just to be able to thank her and shake her hand, it's as simple as that for me.'

LSU and Alabama both entered the game with 6-2 records, with the Tigers ranked No.15 and the Crimson Tide No.9 in the latest AP Rankings.

When Trump canceled his trip to Alabama's game against Georgia a few weeks ago, he vowed to be back to visit them in the future.

Trump wrote on Truth Social: 'Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME! 

'Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia but, hopefully, the Game will go on despite the weather! I will be visiting both of those teams at a later date.'

Alabama lost 20-17 to Georgia then was beaten by Tennessee, but bounced back to beat Texas A&M two weeks ago before an off week.

LSU has beaten Mississippi State and Auburn in impressive fashion in their last two games since a dramatic overtime loss to Kentucky.
news.summary: Melania Trump will be attending LSU's game against Alabama in Baton Rouge, Louisiana this weekend with the First Lady heading to the college football game without the President.

news.title: Trump gets Hanuman Chalisa at White House Diwali
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 7 (IANS) US President Donald Trump received a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa during a Diwali celebration in the Oval Office on Friday (local time), according to entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, who said he presented the devotional text and prayed for friendship between India and America. “Honored to celebrate Diwali with President @realDonaldTrump and proud to gift him with a copy of the Hanuman Chalisa, Tulsidas's hymn to Lord Hanuman that millions of us recite for courage, devotion and strength,” Gondal wrote on X. The White House’s official schedule listed the celebration for 1:30 pm EST in the Oval Office, with no press access. “As the diyas were lit, my prayer was for friendship between India and America, and for the triumph of light over darkness,” Gondal wrote. A photograph showed the cream-coloured book resting against red fabric. Its cover depicted a kneeling Lord Hanuman holding a text, with the title in red lettering, lotus motifs below and metallic protectors on the corners. In a group photograph, guests in Indian attire and dark suits posed around the president’s desk against a backdrop of gold curtains and flags. Books, telephones and a model aircraft stood on the polished desktop. The photographs provided glimpses of the gathering, while Gondal’s posts supplied the account of the gift and lamp-lighting. A photographed programme posted by Gomdal outlined a half-hour ceremony, with presidential remarks and the lighting of a diya scheduled five minutes after the start. Marked “subject to change”, it listed Secretary of State Marco Rubio, FBI Director Kash Patel and National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya among the planned participants. Indian Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra, IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna, Micron Technology chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, chef Vikas Khanna and businesswoman Ruby Dhalla were also listed. Attendance by everyone named in the programme was not independently confirmed. Gondal’s photographs extended beyond the Oval Office, showing guests beside ornate, gold-framed presidential displays and a wall bearing the words “The West Wing” in gold script. He also shared an image of a large coin resting in an open palm. Its black face carried gold-coloured lettering, a central crest and the inscriptions “President of the United States” and “45th & 47th”, surrounded by a silver-coloured rim. “The Trump coin I received this Diwali will always remind me of this day,” he wrote. In a later post, Gondal described the visit in personal terms. “I never imagined celebrating Diwali in the Oval Office. Being there with President Trump, I felt his magnetic presence firsthand,” he wrote. White House Diwali observances began during George W Bush’s administration in 2003. Barack Obama became the first sitting US president to light a diya at the White House in 2009, according to the Obama White House archive. That ceremony took place in the East Room.

news.title: Trump promotes Stephen Miller to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
news.text:
WASHINGTON: - US President Donald Trump replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller on Friday, elevating the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies to run the White House after Republicans lost control of Congress in this week’s midterm elections.

The shake-up puts a longtime Trump loyalist and firebrand policy advisor in charge of steering Trump’s agenda as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate, and an expected wave of congressional investigations.

White House officials told Reuters that Miller’s selection suggests Trump will take an aggressive approach to domestic policy and politics.

Miller is a veteran of Trump’s first term in office in 2017-2021. Since Trump’s return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially been deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he wielded outsize influence across much of Trump’s domestic agenda and has had the ear of the president.

He is perhaps best known for driving Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a target of 3,000 arrests a day. In pursuit of that target, federal immigration agents expanded their list of targets to include migrants who had been living in the US for decades.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors,” and he praised Wiles for doing “an outstanding job.” Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

Wiles, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump’s political operation, according to a White House official.

Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday’s election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be “more aggressive” as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.

Wiles’ allies in the White House began sharing concerns with others on Wednesday about her potential replacement, the person said.

“He’s rewarding those most loyal to him. He’s not changing course,” said another White House official.

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's ICE Under Fire — Senator Demands Answers on Shootings, Chemical Agents and Americans Held in Custody
news.text:
President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown is facing renewed congressional scrutiny after a U.S. senator demanded answers about federal agents shooting civilians, deploying chemical agents and detaining American citizens, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

According to a six-page letter obtained by Radar, Sen. Richard Blumenthal issued 25 sweeping requests to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on November 5, demanding records concerning alleged misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) personnel.Senator Sounds Alarm Over Deadly Enforcement OperationsBlumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, accused the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of engaging in widespread abuses during Trump's immigration enforcement operations.

The Connecticut senator alleged that more than 30 people have been shot and at least nine killed by DHS agents since January 20, 2025, citing previously published reporting. 

He also referenced ProPublica's investigation documenting more than 500 cases involving U.S. citizens detained during the administration's immigration crackdown.

In his letter, Blumenthal accused DHS of deploying armed agents into neighborhoods, conducting immigration sweeps near schools and playgrounds, and using military-style tactics. 

The allegations have not been independently established by the Senate letter, which requests additional government records.DHS Accused of Withholding Critical RecordsBlumenthal claimed his subcommittee had repeatedly attempted to obtain information about immigration enforcement operations without success. He wrote that he had contacted DHS leadership more than a dozen times regarding alleged misconduct.

Despite those requests, Blumenthal alleged the department had "failed to produce a single record responsive to these requests."

The senator is now demanding detailed documentation of enforcement policies, arrest practices, agent training and internal accountability procedures. 

His requests also question whether the White House or DHS implemented arrest quotas and whether agents received financial incentives or promotions tied to detention numbers.Chemical Agents, Shootings and American Citizens Under ScrutinyAmong the most serious demands are records identifying every incident in which ICE or CBP personnel discharged firearms or chemical agents during specified enforcement operations.

Blumenthal wants DHS to identify the locations, circumstances, injuries and justifications associated with those incidents. He is also seeking information about disciplinary action taken against personnel involved in shootings or chemical-agent deployments.

The senator specifically requested a list of U.S. citizens detained for more than 24 hours, including the length of detention, locations and reasons for their arrests. 

Additional demands concern complaints filed by American citizens and instances in which agents used administrative warrants to enter private residences.Homeland Security Faces January DeadlineBlumenthal instructed DHS to begin producing responsive records by November 30, 2026.

He further warned that failure to voluntarily provide the requested documents and information by January 4, 2027, could trigger additional congressional action.

The senator wrote that the subcommittee would have "no choice but to consider alternative measures to obtain compliance." 

The letter does not specify what those measures would involve.

DHS's response to the latest demands was not included in the correspondence.
news.summary: Sen. Richard Blumenthal demands answers from Trump's DHS over ICE shootings, chemical agents and the detention of American citizens.

news.title: Man arrested after Secret Service finds him parked near White House with multiple firearms: Authorities
news.text:
A Venezuelan national was arrested after being found sitting in a stolen vehicle near the White House with several firearms, according to a criminal complaint and the Department of Homeland Security.

The suspect, Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, allegedly threatened to kill President Donald Trump, according to DHS.

A Secret Service officer on patrol spotted the vehicle parked on Constitution Avenue, near the White House complex, shortly before midnight on Thursday, according to the complaint affidavit filed in D.C. Superior Court.

When the officer knocked on the window of the blue Ford F-150 and asked if he was OK and whether he had any weapons, Guanipa-Chrinos allegedly shook his head yes and made a finger gun gesture, according to the affidavit.

After getting out of the vehicle, he allegedly told investigators through Google Translate, "I have the gun because they tried to kill me with it, and I had to take it away from them; it's in the brown bag," according to the affidavit.

According to DHS, Guanipa-Chrinos told officers he "heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump." The affidavit did not include those alleged remarks.

Investigators found a MAC-10 machine pistol, a Glock 43x pistol and an AR-15 rifle in the vehicle, according to the affidavit. There were also "dozens of rounds of ammunition," DHS said.

The vehicle had been reported stolen, according to the affidavit.

Guanipa-Chrinos has been charged with unauthorized use of a vehicle, receiving stolen property, carrying a pistol without a license, carrying a rifle without a license and other firearms charges.

He made an initial appearance in D.C. Superior Court on Friday and remains held without bond, according to online court records.

Guanipa-Chrinos is undocumented and entered the U.S. through Texas in 2024, according to DHS.
news.summary: The suspect, Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, allegedly made threats to kill President Donald Trump, according to DHS.

news.title: Right-Wing ’60 Minutes’ Reporter Busted Grinning With Trump
news.text:
Donald Trump’s crushing midterm defeat didn’t dampen the enthusiasm of the conservative 60 Minutes newcomer tapped to handle the president’s first major post-election interview.

Ross Douthat, who joined CBS in July from The New York Times, was pictured grinning like the Cheshire Cat alongside Trump, 80, behind the Resolute Desk in a photo posted Friday by the White House’s “Rapid Response” X account.

The interview, filmed Friday in the Oval Office, marks Trump’s first one-on-one sit-down since Republicans suffered sweeping election losses Tuesday. It will air Sunday on the beleaguered 60 Minutes, the flagship newsmagazine of MAGA-fied CBS News.

CBS owner and Trump booster David Ellison appointed MAGA-curious Bari Weiss, 42, as editor-in-chief of CBS News in October 2025.

In May and June, Weiss—a former conservative blogger with no broadcast experience—purged a number of the long-running, award-winning 60 Minutes team. 

The interview went to Douthat rather than one of the 60 Minutes veterans who survived Weiss’ spring purge, including Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Jon Wertheim, and Norah O’Donnell.

Stahl, 84, who received the inaugural Daily Beast Power 100 Award on Thursday, said during a speech at the awards luncheon that she considered leaving the program when so many of her colleagues were fired. She ultimately stayed, however, fearing the program would be axed altogether and hoping to protect her remaining colleagues’ jobs.

“There was an urge to walk out in protest and in solidarity with our colleagues who had been abruptly and cruelly fired,” Stahl said.

“But we decided to stay out of a fear, a fear that if we didn’t, 60 Minutes would vanish, and all our colleagues who were still there—producers, editors, so forth—would be let go.”

Since the shake-up, 60 Minutes has been in a ratings slump as viewers shun the latest season, which began in October. 

CBS, meanwhile, offered a considerably less effusive glimpse of the meeting. 

The official 60 Minutes X account posted an “action shot” of Douthat and Trump in conversation, announcing that the interview would cover the GOP’s midterm losses, congressional investigations, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and the economy.

Douthat wasn’t the only Trump-friendly journalist invited into the Oval Office on Friday. 

CNBC anchor Joe Kernen, 70, and his son, Awards Daily reporter Scott Kernen, 24, also stopped by for a grip-and-grin.

CBS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

news.title: China confirms discussions are underway on a historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state.” Nothing is set, but the three-leader gathering would take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

If it happens, it would be historic. Experts, however, say the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds, but they would gather for a photo, with China carefully choreographing the meeting.

“I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content,” said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. “China wants the image but not the costs.”

Beijing is the host of this year’s leaders summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the US and Russia.

Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet Xi for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January.

In a sign that tensions persist, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a Friday video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng urged Beijing to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals,” according to a statement from Greer’s office.

While he’s in China, Trump has said he would be interested in meeting Xi and Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Putin is focused on talking about the war in Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.

“Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former President Barack Obama’s administration.

Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen,” would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Sun of the Stimson Center said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation.”

China also would not engage in talks of arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace is important and wars should end, Sun said.

Beijing’s biggest challenge may be the perception. The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world,” she said.

The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Putin to be seen next to US and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

“But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Singleton said. “The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”
news.summary: Beijing has confirmed discussions about a potential meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, slated to occur this month during a regional summit in Shenzhen. While this gathering could be historic, experts predict that substantial discussions may be unlikely due to conflicting interests, with the meeting primarily serving as a photo opportunity rather than a platform for meaningful diplomatic dialogue.

news.title: Secret Service arrests armed man near White House allegedly threatening to kill Trump
news.text:
(CNN) — The US Secret Service arrested a man near the White House Thursday who allegedly had several guns in a stolen car and was threatening to kill President Donald Trump.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, Secret Service agents noticed Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – a Venezuela national who DHS said entered the US illegally – acting suspiciously in a car along side the White House.

“When they confronted the suspect, he said that he heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump,” DHS said in a news release. “The officers then discovered that the vehicle had been reported stolen, and the suspect admitted to having weapons in his vehicle.”

The agents discovered a rifle and two handguns along with dozens of rounds of ammunition in the car, DHS said.

Chrinos was arrested on numerous firearms charges as well as unauthorized use of a vehicle and receiving stolen property.

He is currently in the custody of the US Marshals Service. DHS said Chrinos entered the US illegally in 2024.

“This is the latest example of Secret Service personnel relying on extensive training and experience to deescalate a volatile situation that posed an imminent threat to our protectees and other Americans,” said US Secret Service Director Sean Curran. “This incident reflects the heightened threat environment in which we operate, as well as the continued number of armed individuals who are drawn to the White House complex.”

According to the Secret Service, the White House has seen a significant uptick in instances involving mental health issues. The White House and presidency, officials say, can act as a symbolic focal point for people with such issues.

In May, Secret Service officers shot and killed a man with previous mental health issues after he opened fire near a security checkpoint at the White House.

news.title: US measles death toll rises to eight
news.text:
Eight measles-related deaths have been reported across the US this year after an infant died in Wisconsin, marking the country’s deadliest outbreak of the disease in decades, according to state health department figures.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services announced the death on Thursday, the state’s first measles-related fatality since 1990, as an outbreak continues in its southwestern counties.

Pennsylvania has recorded six deaths, while New York has reported one, with three of the fatalities announced this week.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, has officially recorded only four measles-related deaths this year, reflecting a discrepancy between federal and state reporting figures.

According to the CDC’s latest figures, 5,182 infections had been confirmed nationwide as of this Thursday, more than double the 2,289 recorded throughout 2025.

Wisconsin alone had reported 431 cases across 13 counties as of November 3, its highest total in more than 35 years.

Pennsylvania has been particularly hard hit, with nearly 1,500 cases reported since an outbreak began in April.

Health authorities have urged residents to check their vaccination status and receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine if necessary.

The resurgence has raised questions about whether the US could lose its measles elimination status, granted in 2000 after sustained domestic transmission of the virus was halted. The Pan American Health Organization is expected to review the country’s status next week.

Health authorities have linked the spread of the highly contagious disease to declining vaccination rates. CDC data show that coverage among kindergarteners has fallen from 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025-2026.

In August, President Donald Trump signed an executive order calling for separating the combined MMR vaccine into individual shots, drawing criticism from medical groups warning that the move could discourage vaccination.

The CDC recommends two doses of the combined MMR vaccine, which it says provides approximately 97% protection against measles.

The disease typically causes fever, coughing, a runny nose and a rash, but can also lead to life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Children under five, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems face particularly high risks.

Before widespread vaccination began in the 1960s, measles claimed up to 500 lives annually in the US, according to CDC estimates.

Eight measles-related deaths have been reported across the US in 2026 after an infant died in Wisconsin amid a nationwide outbreak
