news.text: US President Donald Trump has appointed Stephen Miller, one of his closest political aides and the driving force behind several of his hardline immigration policies, as the new White House chief of staff.Announcing the decision on Truth Social on Friday, Trump described the 41-year-old as 'one of my most trusted advisors'. Miller will replace Susie Wiles and assume charge on Monday. The appointment comes days after Republicans suffered a setback in the midterm elections, with Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January. Miller’s elevation places a key figure behind Trump’s immigration agenda at the centre of White House operations, even as his role in controversial policies is likely to attract greater scrutiny from congressional Democrats. From Conservative Activist To Trump Aide Miller developed his conservative credentials during his school and university years. At Santa Monica High School, he criticised what he considered liberal policies on local radio programmes. At Duke University, he led the Duke Conservative Union and defended three lacrosse players accused of rape.After graduating, he worked as a legislative aide to Republican lawmakers, including Senator Jeff Sessions. He joined Trump's presidential campaign in January 2016 and became instrumental in shaping his speeches and political messaging. Following Trump's election victory, Miller served as a senior adviser and speechwriter. He helped formulate the administration's 2018 'Zero Tolerance' border policy, which led to thousands of migrant children being separated from their parents. He also advocated ending the DACA programme and supported the 2017 travel restrictions targeting several Muslim-majority countries.His political positions drew criticism after the Southern Poverty Law Center published emails in 2019 that it said showed his support for white nationalist websites and ideologies. He has also defended aggressive immigration enforcement operations and Trump's attempts to restrict birthright citizenship.Miller has backed the administration's actions against individuals accused of undermining US foreign policy through their support for Palestinian rights. He has also defended Trump's military actions abroad, supported the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and argued that the US could assert control over Greenland through military power. news.title: Iran Distributes Iodine Tablets Near Nuclear Sites Amid Fears Of Possible US Strikes: Report

Iran has begun distributing iodine tablets to people living near its nuclear facilities amid concerns that the United States could launch fresh military strikes against the country, according to a report by The Times of London, which cited an Iranian Health Ministry official.
"Yes, we are distributing iodine," the official was quoted as saying. "Trump can no longer be trusted. He may go through with this crime," Al Jazeera reported.
The official said Iranian authorities had routinely distributed the preventive medication to residents living within a two-to-three-kilometre radius of nuclear installations during periods of heightened military conflict.
The reported move comes as US President Donald Trump weighs whether to resume military operations against Iran, with American officials confirming that his national security team has held discussions on the issue.

An Iranian political journalist told The Times that state officials had been informed during a recent briefing that a possible US strike on the heavily fortified Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site was being given serious consideration.
The reports have added to concerns in Iran over the possibility of renewed military escalation.

news.title: 'Defeated Goliath': Did faith help Democrats flip key midterm races?
news.text:
As Democrat James Talarico of Texas delivered his acceptance speech Tuesday in Austin after his decisive U.S. Senate race win over Republican Ken Paxton, a large placard in front of him featured the words, “Love Thy Neighbor.”

That message seemed to resonate with voters nationwide, who vastly backed Democrats in a sweeping series of victories that some saw as a humanitarian rejection of federal policies such as overly aggressive immigration enforcement, unauthorized war, efforts to stamp out diversity and economic measures that have left many families struggling.

Religion proved pivotal at the ballot box nationwide, experts say, shaping voter views on key issues that turned previously red states blue. Faith was also brandished by candidates like Talarico to appeal to the electorate, even as conservatives blasted his progressive Christianity; in some cases, religion was weaponized by opponents, as in Islamophobic attacks and ad campaigns in Michigan and Texas.

“You did see some rejection of Republicans, especially with Hispanic Catholics in Texas,” said Michael Moreland, director of the Eleanor H. McCullen Center for Law, Religion and Public Policy at Villanova University in Pennsylvania. “Especially along the South Texas border, aspects of the administration’s immigration enforcement alienated a lot of voters. President Trump in 2024 peeled off a lot of those voters, but he lost them Tuesday night.”

Democrat megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton was elected both the state’s first Jewish and female governor, her Judaism informing her progressive platform.

Meanwhile, a record seven Muslims were elected to Congress nationwide, including Democrat physician Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who became the nation’s first Muslim U.S. senator. The number could rise to eight, depending on how California Democrat Aisha Wahab fares in her race for the state’s 14th Congressional district seat.

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and grandson of a Baptist preacher, was among several candidates who charted rare territory for white Democrats by making religion a central part of his campaign, citing scripture and stressing his Biblical grounding.

Dubbed “Talafreako” by President Donald Trump, Talarico kicked off his acceptance speech by using the Bible story of David and Goliath as a metaphor for his race against Paxton and “billionaire megadonors” like Elon Musk, who spent nearly $230 million to support Paxton’s campaign against Talarico.

“We went up against our own Goliath – the richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire D.C. establishment,” Talarico said. Comparing himself to the shepherd boy who wielded a slingshot to slay his mightier foe, he told the crowd: “You were my slingshot. The people of Texas were my slingshot. And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”

Swing to Dems more pronounced among some faiths

Nationwide, exit polls conducted by NBC News revealed sizable shifts among several groups in the midterms compared to the 2024 election. Just under half of Catholics backed Republican candidates in the midterms, NBC found, compared to 59% who voted for Trump in 2024.

Jewish voters, meanwhile, swung the other way, NBC found: While 78% supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024, 68% voted for Democrats in this year’s midterms.

"Donald Trump said voters should pretend he was on the ballot in the midterms, and Jewish Americans did just that," Halie Soifer, CEO of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, said in a statement. "Jewish voters are not a monolith, but they widely disapprove of Donald Trump. This, coupled with the strength of the Democratic candidates who flipped red seats blue, led to overwhelming support for Democrats among Jewish voters in this election.”

Among religiously unaffiliated voters, NBC found, 27% supported Trump in 2024, compared to 20% who favored Republican candidates this fall.

Meanwhile, 86% of Muslims supported Democratic candidates in 2026 – the share wasn’t tallied in 2024 – while slightly fewer Protestants or other Christians supported Republican candidates this year compared with 2024.

Exit polls conducted by the Council on American-Islamic Relations indicated the Iran war, the economy, rising Islamophobia and Israel’s war in Gaza were foremost in their midterm voting choices. “Rising Islamophobia strengthened their motivation to vote,” the council said in a statement. “They overwhelmingly backed Democrats, but many remain unconvinced that either party listens to their concerns.”

During his race for Michigan’s Senate seat, El-Sayed was dismissed as a “jihadist” by Trump and accused of links to terrorist groups, both without evidence. Others criticized him for what they saw as a failure to sufficiently denounce antisemitism.

Frank Lacopo, an assistant professor of history at Southeast Missouri State University in Cape Girardeau, said such comments backfired with voters concerned with other issues.

“It really seems like El-Sayed’s more secular messaging on affordability was more effective,” Lacopo said. “What he showed people in Michigan was a vision of an American who happens to be Muslim.”

Did Catholics feel betrayed by Trump, GOP?

More than 50 million Catholics live in the U.S., with about 53% identifying as Republican, according to the Pew Research Center. Accounting for about a quarter of U.S. voters, they represent a broad political spectrum.

“It’s hard to neatly categorize the Catholic vote, because it depends on other factors – whether they’re white Catholics, Hispanic Catholics, young Catholics or more churchgoing ones,” Moreland said.

Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of Catholic Vote, a conservative political advocacy organization based in Carmel, Indiana, said Catholics’ midterm swing toward Democrats reflected the broad concerns of the American electorate.

“In this election, Catholics are representative of the American population writ large,” Reinhardt said. “They care about necessities. The socioeconomic stratosphere of Catholics is pretty ordinary.”

In 2024, she said, Catholic voters largely believed Trump would be a greater arbiter of Catholic values. This time around, some may have felt betrayed by Trump’s broken anti-war promises, while anti-abortion advocates likely felt the president hasn’t done enough to advance their cause.

“The Catholic vote is soft Republican when there’s a Republican who advances their ideals,” Reinhardt said. “But they swing back when they feel their values are not being met. The Iran war was a factor too, but I’m not sure whether it’s an issue because it was declared immoral by the pope or because people didn’t want a forever war.”

Catholic concerns loomed large at the state level, such as in Virginia, where local bishops led a furious campaign that unsuccessfully sought to mobilize voters to reject ballot measures expanding abortion rights and removing wordage in the state constitution strictly defining marriage as between a man and woman.

“That was one where Catholics were heroic in their efforts,” Reinhardt said. “But 700,000 Catholics in Virginia won’t overturn the majority there.”

Lacopo thinks a factor that may have been a factor in Catholics’ Democratic swing is the Catholic church’s growing presence online.

“It’s important not to underestimate the power that Catholic church messaging on social media has on Catholics,” he said. “Even if they’re not practicing Catholics. A lot of Americans began to subscribe to Vatican News when Leo became pope, and they identify with him as an American.”

Pope Leo XIV’s fluency in both English and Spanish allows him to reach a wide swath of voters, he said. Meanwhile, the pope’s social media features a constant feed of direct quotes from the Chicago-born pontiff that help American followers see him as someone representing “a more accepting, open-arms version of Christianity.”

In general, Lacopo feels Democrats fielded better quality candidates who appealed to voters, with faith part of the package in states like Texas and Kansas.

“Talarico was absolutely perfect as a candidate for Texas because he had a way of speaking that came from his background of training as a Presbyterian minister,” Lacopo said. “He was able to use Christian messaging in a way that couldn’t be countered by Republicans.”

He noted Talarico’s acceptance speech also focused on what many consider the central tenets of Christian teaching, the notion of loving God and one’s neighbor – a message he thinks resonated not just with Texas Latinos anxious over immigration policy but with the kind of voters who plant signs reading “No Human Being is Illegal” in their front yards.

“I’m surprised and not surprised at the same time that Democrats have taken so long to latch on to that,” Lacopo said. “Even if you’re a secular voter and don’t practice religion, you can relate to the second part of that message.”

news.title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña Ousted & Placed Under House Arrest After Ueno Bank Collapse; Vice President Sworn In As Successor
news.text: Asuncion: Ousted Paraguay president Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies. The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, cutting nearly three million customers off from their savings and bank cards and setting off a political crisis.Prosecutors ordered that Peña be held at his home until he can be brought before their economic crimes and anti-corruption unit, according to a letter to the national police commander. The attorney general's office confirmed to The Associated Press that he had been detained there.The order also called for the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, the former central bank chief Peña appointed. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo was in custody. Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing.Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term, which ends in August 2028. He inherits a government under pressure to return depositors' money and punish those behind Ueno's collapse.A veteran of the long-ruling conservative Colorado party, Alliana, 52, is a former governor of the southern province of Ñeembucú and a former speaker of the lower house. He has not escaped the scandal entirely: Prosecutors are also investigating him, and on Thursday lawmakers shelved an opposition bid to impeach him.Peña's removal bars him from the lifetime Senate seat granted to elected former presidents under Paraguay's Constitution, denying him the parliamentary immunity that would accompany it. Prosecutors are also investigating current and former central bank and pension fund officials.Donald Trump Appoints Stephen Miller As White House Chief Of Staff, Susie Wiles Moves To Political Operation Amid Democratic Gains In Congress Peña had submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it. His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that lawmakers should have approved his departure instead of pressing ahead with the impeachment trial. Opposition lawmakers insisted on removal to prevent him from leaving office with immunity."He must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison," opposition Sen Yolanda Paredes told reporters. "The public is fed up with impunity."In a farewell message released shortly before the verdict Friday, Peña expressed hope his departure would spare Paraguay further harm."I do not want my presence to be a cause of greater division or instability," he wrote. "My responsibility is to put the country above my personal fate."Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day. Thousands of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno's failure have clashed with police firing rubber bullets and pepper spray this week. Paraguay's largest teachers' union, which has more than 40,000 members, plans to begin an indefinite national strike Monday to press for protection of public pension funds.Marco Rubio Dismisses Trump Administration Exit Rumours, Reaffirms Commitment To Serving Full Term Amid 2028 Presidential Speculation "This was an enormous betrayal of trust," said Yinal López, a worker at the state electricity company, whose employee pension fund also had money at Ueno. "The president made a mockery of the people. He used their money, the people's money, to do whatever he wanted."Bank collapse becomes political reckoningUeno's implosion has plunged Paraguay into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade - and at dizzying speed. Regulators seized the bank before dawn Tuesday.By Thursday afternoon, Peña had offered to resign as his conservative Colorado party turned on him, led by former President Horacio Cartes, the party chief and Peña's longtime mentor. By Friday, his interior minister, chief of staff, legal adviser and political adviser had all quit.It was a staggering reversal of fortunes for Peña, a telegenic technocrat and a former International Monetary Fund economist who owed his rapid political ascent to Cartes. The tobacco magnate, among Paraguay's richest men, made Peña his finance minister and twice backed him for president over rival factions' objections.Once in office, though, Peña quietly amassed a rival power base, analysts say. Ueno Bank, flush with public deposits, became the centerpiece of both his business empire and his effort to win over provincial governors as he sought to escape Cartes' shadow.Who Is Harmeet Kaur Dhillon? Indian-Origin Woman Resigns As US Civil Rights Chief, First Senior Trump Aide To Exit After Midterm Setback "It's like a Shakespearean drama. He tried to displace his mentor, his political patron," said Miguel Carter, director of DEMOS, a Paraguayan research centre. "But he did so on very fragile grounds."Cartes struck back. In September, senators loyal to him demanded answers from the central bank about Ueno's lending, citing leaked internal reports that warned its loans to related companies put its solvency at risk. When Ueno collapsed this week, so did Peña's leverage, and Cartes, once sanctioned by the US Treasury over alleged corruption, publicly called for the ouster of his erstwhile protégé."Cartes put the nail in the coffin," said Andrew Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham. "Peña had no political base to rely on, and he was left high and dry."A bank built on public moneyUeno rose from obscurity to become Paraguay's fifth-largest bank by deposits in just a few years, with more than USD 800 million in public money turbocharging its expansion. It signed up more than two-thirds of the country's adults, its splashy logo appearing everywhere from the national soccer stadium to street vendors' bank cards.The impeachment charges cite Peña's stake in Ueno's holding company, which he divested under pressure last year, and his appointment of a former Ueno executive to run the central bank that regulated it. Lawmakers also accuse him of letting the state pension fund deposit USD 355 million at the bank, beyond legal limits.Bangladesh Garment Workers' Strike Sparks Violence In Savar & Ashulia, Over 200 Factories Declare Holidays Analysts say those high-level connections helped shield Ueno from regulatory scrutiny even as concerns about its finances grew."For the last 20 years, the central bank has been one of the two pillars that gave Paraguay international credibility in managing its economy," said José Tomás Sánchez, a political theory professor at the National University of Asunción. "And under Peña, it began to lose credibility, lose neutrality and then relax all its control mechanisms to favor the business group that had Ueno Bank as one of its pillars."Frozen accounts, rising angerOvernight, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say their accounts are frozen."The ripple effect on the general population has been immense," Nickson said. "That has fueled the ire of many people in Paraguay who are not particularly politically aware or very interested in politics."Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about USD 1,600). Deposits are insured up to about USD 37,000, which the central bank says covers nearly all of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.Prosecutors have charged 27 people, including Ueno's controlling shareholder, Miguel Vázquez, with crimes including breach of trust and attempted fraud, and six bank directors are in pretrial detention. Authorities have seized nine luxury cars from Vázquez's home, along with a yacht and small planes linked to him, and searched executives' homes in a gated community outside the capital. news.title: Trump offers Democrats immigration, tax talks
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 7 (IANS) US President Donald Trump opened the door to working with Democrats on immigration and taxes after Republican midterm losses, identifying economic development as another area for cooperation. Asked which Democratic initiatives he could support, Trump said there were several possibilities. “I think a lot. I mean, I said before, immigration’s one, tax cuts, or maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient and better,” he told reporters during an evening airport gaggle in Florida. “A lot of economic development initiatives we can do. I think we can do a lot of things together.” Trump said some newly elected politicians wanted to meet him to discuss issues affecting their states. He mentioned Texas and South Carolina but did not identify the politicians or announce meetings. His comments signalled a willingness to negotiate without setting out the immigration changes or tax measures he would support. He did not endorse a particular Democratic bill. There was no specific pledge on H-1B visas, employment-based green cards or other provisions affecting Indian professionals and families. The president’s conciliatory remarks came alongside criticism of Congress over stalled legislation. Asked what he wanted accomplished before the new Congress took office, Trump urged senators from both parties to act. He accused Democrats of voting as a bloc and some Republicans of obstructing legislation, while calling on Senate Republican leader John Thune to get measures moving. Trump also pointed to judges and other nominees awaiting confirmation. He offered no legislative timetable for the immigration, tax or economic-development discussions. The president acknowledged that Republicans had suffered a bad election, blaming Senate inaction and higher oil prices among other factors. He sought to distance himself from the outcome by noting that he had not been on the ballot. His offer to discuss policy with Democrats came on the day he named Stephen Miller as his next White House chief of staff. During the gaggle, Trump praised Miller’s loyalty and dismissed suggestions that the change reflected dissatisfaction with his team over the election results. The November 3 midterm elections determined the membership of the next Congress, which takes office in January. Until then, the outgoing Congress remains responsible for legislation and Senate consideration of presidential nominations.

news.text: US President Donald Trump has hinted that more senior officials could leave his administration following the Republican Party's crushing defeat in the midterm elections, saying he may make "a few changes" to his Cabinet. news.title: Secret phone blitz on Stephen Miller’s behalf greased his path to new job: report
news.text:
Stephen Miller's rise to the top of President Donald Trump's White House got a quiet push from someone very close to home.

Katie Miller, Stephen Miller's wife, spent weeks urging people in Trump's orbit to call the president and pitch her husband as Susie Wiles' successor before Trump tapped him for chief of staff, Politico reported Friday, citing two people with direct knowledge of her role.

Her outreach picked up after Tuesday's election, when Republicans suffered a stinging midterm defeat. She placed roughly six calls to figures close to Trump, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and several people in Vice President JD Vance's circle, according to two people familiar with the calls.

She told those she reached that her husband should be the pick if Wiles stepped aside, adding, "I would appreciate if you could share that message," according to one person with direct knowledge. 

The effort played out while the White House was loudly denying that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Politico Playbook reported in October that the president had been sounding out friends about possible successors.

People familiar with Katie Miller's calls told the outlet she never pushed to have Wiles removed, and that her most recent round came only once it was obvious Trump wanted a new chief of staff.

"He started telling people he was done with Susie," one source said of the days after the election. "This is what happens when you get creamed."

Other names Trump privately discussed included Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, special envoy Steve Witkoff, former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and New York Yankees President Randy Levine, while Lee Zeldin and Sergio Gor were also mentioned. One White House adviser said the idea of Pulte running the West Wing had rattled many in the Trump administration.

Discontent with Wiles had been simmering throughout the campaign, but the GOP's drubbing effectively ended her tenure, according to the report.

"There was just no saving Susie. She knew that," said one person close to the White House.

Wiles, who recently went through chemotherapy for breast cancer, had already been weighing an exit after the midterms, two other sources said.

"She loves the job — it’s the job of a lifetime, but you have no life," one of them said.

Katie Miller, who declined to comment, worked at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump's first term and later joined Elon Musk's DOGE operation before launching a podcast featuring top administration officials. The White House did not immediately respond to Politico's request for comment.

news.title: Trump weighs Iran’s fate after midterm rout
news.text:
US president says world will ‘know very soon’ whether he makes a deal with Tehran or orders strikes• Calls Qatar’s Sheikh Tamim as Doha steps up its mediation• Centcom prepares for possible return to fight

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump is said to be weighing whether to resume large-scale strikes against Iran after Democrats’ sweeping victory in rec-ent midterm elections, even as he opened a new diplomatic channel on Friday by calling Qatar’s emir to discuss efforts to end the eight-month-old conflict.

The call with Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani came amid an intensifying regional diplomatic effort to prevent another round of major hostilities. But Trump has continued to keep military action on the table, saying on Thursday that the world would “know very soon” whether he would make a deal with Tehran or order new strikes to “destroy what is left” of the country.

“I would prefer not to destroy what is left of the country, if possible, but I may have to do so,” Trump told reporters, adding that Iran could take 25 years to reb-uild from the damage already inflicted.

Friday’s conversation with the Qatari leader focused on diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions. Sheikh Tamim’s office said he had emphasised dialogue and diplomatic means to resolve disputes and prevent further escalation.

Qatar has been playing a key intermediary role in efforts to negotiate an agreement between Washington and Tehran.

Trump’s latest moves illustrate the dilemma confronting him after the Republican party’s midterm debacle. Democrats have won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, giving them an opportunity to challenge his policies during the final two years of his presidency.

The Iran war contributed to the Republican defeat, particularly because of its impact on gasoline prices and the wider cost of living. While both Trump and his Vice President JD Vance acknowledged its political consequences, the former defended his decision to launch the conflict.

“If I had to do it again, I’d do it again,” he said after the election. VP Vance was more direct, writing on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.

In an Oval Office exchange on Thursday, Trump nevertheless suggested that the election results would not deter him from military action. “If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in,” he said.

The president has several options: he could maintain the present military posture, continue the naval blockade restricting Iranian oil exports, or launch another campaign targeting Iran’s remaining military and strategic infrastructure. A negotiated settlement involving the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief and renewed nuclear talks remains another possibility, one which the rest of the world is far more keen on.

US media reports suggest Centcom is preparing for a possible return to major combat operations, although it has not received an order to begin them.

Meanwhile, diplomacy has accelerated in the Middle East, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi holding calls with counterparts from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt this week. Qatari mediators have discussed reciprocal confidence-building measures, including a possible US easing of its naval blockade and release of frozen Iranian funds in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear negotiations.

Senior diplomats in Washington say they do not expect an immediate change in the administration’s foreign policy. Military preparations and peace efforts are likely to continue simultaneously.

They believe the election has increased, rather than diminished, Pakistan’s importance as a potential peacemaker. Islamabad and other regional capitals, however, are waiting for the dust to settle in Washington, including uncertainty over the future of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, before launching another diplomatic initiative.

Frederick Kempe, president of the Atlantic Council, warned that the election outcome could make negotiations more difficult.

“In the Gulf, the consequences could be more immediate, as Iranians will interpret the outcome as a vote against Trump’s war and will be even more reluctant to negotiate the future of their nuclear capabilities,” Kempe wrote.

In the absence of an unexpected Iranian decision to accept a negotiated settlement, Kempe considered a sustained series of US strikes designed to degrade Iran’s remaining military capabilities and damage its energy infrastructure a likely scenario. “This could provide Trump with an opportunity to declare that the United States’ principal military objectives have been achieved,” he wrote.

Trump’s threat that US might eventually have to “give them the hammer”, however, suggests that another operation could go beyond limited punitive strikes. A further escalation could invite Iranian retaliation against American bases, Gulf infrastructure and commercial shipping.

A strike against the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility has also been discussed as a possible option. But even if the United States declares its military objectives achieved, the underlying questions surrounding Iran’s nuclear programme and regional security would remain unresolved.

The election has also strengthened Democrats’ ability to challenge the administration’s conduct of the war. They will assume control of congressional committees and spending decisions when the new Congress convenes in January.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has already called for an end to the conflict. “This war must end. It must end,” he said, pointing to Congress’s power over government spending as a means of restraining military operations.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries also urged Trump to end the war before the new Congress takes office, blaming the conflict for increasing fuel, fertiliser and grocery costs. “We ran on affordability. We won on affordability,” he said.

According to the AP Voter Poll, about six in ten voters considered the decision to take military action against Iran wrong. However, only about one-third said the war was crucial in determining their congressional vote, compared with roughly half who identified the cost of living and government corruption as major considerations.

The economic consequences remain a significant constraint on Trump’s choices. GasBuddy put the US national average gasoline price at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday and early Friday, although analysts expect it could fall below $4 next week. Markets had initially responded to the election results with lower oil prices amid expectations that Washington would face greater pressure to negotiate.

Elisa Ewers, a senior fellow for Middle East studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, believes Trump’s domestic political difficulties could produce a more aggressive foreign policy. “Trump may take on an even more adventurist foreign policy, including in the Middle East, as he faces real constraints on his domestic agenda,” she wrote.

news.title: Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene
news.text:
The stage is set for a historic showdown inside Chicago’s federal courthouse, where a judge has ordered the city’s top federal prosecutor to testify — and made clear she doesn’t believe what he’s told her about the disastrous “Broadview Six” scandal.

U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros is due on the witness stand later this month. So are three prosecutors from his office. Sanctions and criminal contempt charges loom. And finger-pointing has already begun over the failed 2025 prosecution of six Midway Blitz protesters.

U.S. District Judge April Perry’s hearing could take the Dirksen Federal Courthouse deep into uncharted waters — if it goes down. That remains to be seen, thanks in large part to a new character in the case: Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward.

Woodward is the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official. He’s increasingly at the center of Justice Department controversies, and he appears to have taken the wheel in the Broadview Six litigation. He publicly inserted himself into the case Oct. 30.

Woodward is expected to challenge Perry and try to short-circuit her hearing, which she’s said will take place by Nov. 24. No such challenge has surfaced yet, though, and the Justice Department has declined to comment.

The day Woodward entered the Broadview Six case, Woodward also faced off with U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington. The pair tangled over a golf course President Donald Trump has sought to renovate in the nation’s capital, in an exchange that seemed to solidify Woodward’s defiant reputation.

The exasperated Reyes told Woodward early on, “let’s not play games anymore,” according to a transcript of the hearing.

That did little to bring the temperature down.

They parried over “word games” and social media posts. At one point, the judge accused Woodward of trying to take back an argument he’d made.

“Here’s the thing,” she told Woodward, “you just said it. There’s literally a transcript of it. Now, if you want to correct yourself and say ‘gosh, that’s not what I meant,’ by all means.”

“Gosh, that’s not what I meant,” Woodward replied.

Later, the judge asked Woodward about the golf course itself. She told him, “you’re the one who’s a golfer, not me.”

“I have golfed,” Woodward replied. “I would not describe myself as a golfer.”

Particularly frustrating to the judge, it seemed, was Woodward’s refusal to interpret Truth Social messages from Trump.

“We’re not on TV,” Woodward told her. “I mean, I’m not a pundit opining about the president’s words.

“As you’ve reminded me multiple times, I’m the No. 3 ranking official at the Department of Justice.”

And now, Woodward’s at the center of the “Broadview Six” case.

What does Judge Perry want to know?

Perry made her purpose clear during a hearing Oct. 1: “My sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.”

In other words, she wants to know whether she was lied to during the Broadview Six prosecution.

The case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.

But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.

The case collapsed after Perry discovered apparent misconduct by Boutros’ staff while they sought an indictment against the group from a grand jury. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg allegedly spoke to grand jurors outside the grand jury room, for example.

While the initial controversy revolved around Mecklenburg’s alleged misconduct, Perry has since turned her attention to the accuracy of two claims made by the feds last spring.

The first revolved around whether the White House played any role in the case. Boutros’ team told Perry in March there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside [the U.S. attorney’s office] (other than the local FBI investigators assigned to the case) regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.

“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House” or at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, prosecutors wrote.

That claim has been undermined by a recent lawsuit brought against Boutros by former Chicago FBI boss Douglas DePodesta.

It alleges that Boutros met in DePodesta’s office Oct. 7, 2025, with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald. Blanche is now the attorney general.

“During this meeting, Defendant Boutros discussed the Broadview Six investigation with his superiors in the Department of Justice and other law enforcement officers,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.

That meeting would have happened two days before Boutros’ office first tried to secure an indictment against the Broadview Six.

The judge has also zeroed in on Boutros’ claim that he learned of alleged wrongdoing by Mecklenburg in late April. He’s since acknowledged receiving a transcript in October 2025 that documented some of her alleged misconduct.

Boutros said he didn’t remember reading it.

But grand jurors initially rejected the Broadview Six case. The feds went back to the panel twice, records show. And Perry pointed out that “Boutros himself had to approve the re-presentment of the case to the grand jury.”

“The idea that [U.S. Attorney] Boutros would have made such a significant decision without reviewing the best evidence available to him about what went wrong in the grand jury is nearly unfathomable,” Perry wrote.

Who is Stanley Woodward?

Woodward entered the Broadview Six case fresh off his showdown with Judge Reyes in Washington. But he’s been at the center of other recent Justice Department controversies. 

In May, Woodward signed the settlement agreement between the president and the IRS that established the controversial “anti-weaponization fund” for people claiming to be harmed by “lawfare” and the weaponization of the justice system.

He signed that deal three days before the Broadview Six case collapsed. Members of the group actually once mused about applying to the fund — but Blanche later issued an order insisting the fund was rescinded “beyond any doubt.”

Woodward’s name also appears at the top of the Justice Department’s Oct. 22 lawsuit over an entry into the Alaska Senate race by a candidate with a similar name to Sen. Dan Sullivan. That lawsuit has already been tossed by a judge, though the Justice Department has filed an appeal.

In addition to his battles with Judge Reyes, Woodward has also moved to disqualify judges in Minnesota. He alleged one made “unethical” comments to The New York Times about the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.

“The American people will undoubtedly question” whether the judge can be impartial, Woodward wrote.

Finally, upon entering Chicago’s Broadview Six case, Woodward told Judge Perry she should clarify whether a previous “request” she’d made for records was really meant to be a “directive.”

But “for the avoidance of doubt,” he wrote, “the United States has not agreed to provide any information.”

And, he made clear, “the United States believes further proceedings would not be appropriate.”

What will happen at the hearing?

There’s no obvious playbook for Perry’s hearing. So attorneys have already begun to question how it would go forward.

In addition to Boutros, Perry ordered three rank-and-file prosecutors who worked the Broadview Six case to take the stand: William Hogan, Matthew Skiba and Andres Almendarez.

Their attorneys declined to comment beyond briefs filed in court.

In her order Monday, Perry said testimony will revolve around grand jury transcripts in the case, the accuracy of statements made to her by the feds, and “prosecutors’ repeated failures to correct the court’s stated misconceptions about the aforementioned matters.”

She also invited “any former or current employee of the U.S. attorney’s office or federal law enforcement agency who has first-hand knowledge about the above events” to testify.

That’s been taken as a likely reference to DePodesta or Mecklenburg. DePodesta attorney Ron Safer told the Chicag oSun-Times that his client’s information is likely “tangential” to Perry’s investigation. Mecklenburg’s attorney declined to comment.

Hogan attorney Shelly Kulwin raised questions in a filing this week about who will be questioning the prosecutors and whether cross-examination will be allowed. Kulwin also asked whether he’ll be allowed to present his own evidence.

In an order responding to Kulwin on Friday, Perry said, “Each witness will be asked to speak about the issues” raised in her Monday order “of which they have personal knowledge.”

Perry wrote that she “will ask follow-up questions, if necessary. No cross-examination by other witnesses or their attorneys will be permitted.”

No other witnesses may be called, she wrote, beyond the invitation she’d already extended.

Finally, she said she’d eventually be willing to hear evidence in favor of certain individuals, if at a later point, she “determine[s] that court-imposed sanctions are likely.”

news.title: Ted Cruz Says Democrats Are 'Drunk on Their Own Power' After Midterm Wins
news.text: Senator Ted Cruz said Democrats are "drunk on their own power" after their midterm victories, predicting the party will overreach despite what he described as a "generationally damaging" defeat for Republicans. Speaking on his Verdict podcast Friday, the Texas Republican argued Democratic leaders will interpret their gains as a mandate for a broader progressive agenda, even though he believes voters were primarily expressing frustration over economic concerns. "These guys are drunk on their own power," Cruz said. "They are high on their own supply." Cruz claims Democratic leaders are already misreading the election results. "The radicals are running the Democrat Party," he said. "They believe they have a mandate." The comments came as Cruz assessed the scale of Republican losses nationwide, which handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and expanded the party's Senate majority. "We're already at 54 Democrats. We could be at 56," Cruz said. "That is generationally damaging." Cruz argued Senate defeats are particularly difficult to overcome because senators serve six-year terms, potentially locking in Democratic gains for years. "It will take six years to have the chance to turn them around," he said. "Retaking the majority in the Senate is very, very difficult." Texas political analyst Scott Braddock, editor of Quorum Report, offered a different interpretation on his show, arguing Democrats won because James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa and other candidates remained focused on voters' economic concerns. "Republicans kept trying to bait them into having arguments about culture wars," Braddock said on his podcast. Instead, he said, Democrats stayed "laser focused" on affordability and the economy. "It's the economy, stupid, and guess what? It still is." What Happened in Texas? Democrats swept every statewide race in Republicans' most populous stronghold Tuesday, ending a three-decade losing streak. Talarico, Democratic state representative, defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had President Donald Trump's support, despite a series of scandals. Hinojosa, also a state representative, upset three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the state's first Hispanic governor. In the lieutenant governor's race, Democratic state lawmaker Vikki Goodwin ousted Republican incumbent Dan Patrick. Meanwhile, Democratic state Senator Nathan Johnson won the attorney general's race over Republican state Senator Mayes Middleton. Republican Bo French, who drew condemnation from members of his own party over remarks about University of Texas students, lost the race for railroad commissioner to Democratic state Representative Jon Rosenthal. And all of these defeats came after Republicans' redistricting efforts aimed at bolstering the GOP's chance at winning five additional seats. Ted Cruz as Trump's Ally Cruz, who has represented Texas in the Senate since 2013, is one of the best-known and most polarizing politicians in the state. A former Texas solicitor general and 2016 presidential candidate, Cruz built his national profile as a leading voice in the conservative movement and a close ally of Trump after initially running against him in the Republican primary. While Cruz remains popular among many Republican voters, he has also drawn criticism from Democrats and some independents, particularly following his 2021 trip to Cancun during a deadly Texas winter storm and his role challenging the 2020 presidential election results. Dozens of critics posted in responses to his podcast that he was misinterpreting the election results and that he would be the next Republican voted out of office in Texas. Cruz Predicts a Republican Rebound in 2028 While acknowledging the severity of the midterm losses, Cruz said he believes Democrats will ultimately undermine their own position by focusing on policies voters were not demanding. The senator said that Democrats campaigned heavily on affordability and economic frustrations but will now pursue priorities that are disconnected from what motivated voters to support them this year. "The people who were pissed and understandably pissed and said, 'I'm mad at you, I'm voting the other side,' every issue they were mad about is going to get worse," Cruz said. Cruz also addressed the political implications for Texas, where Democrats made historic gains during the 2026 cycle. He argued that while the state's political landscape has shifted, Republicans can win back voters if Democrats fail to deliver on economic issues. "I think 2028 is going to be a really good Republican year," he said. "Ironically, because 2026 was such a bad Republican year."
